item.title: Accumulating Pruning Constraints: New Exact Polynomial-Space Algorithms for Max 2-SAT
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: max-cut

Authors: Konstantin Kutzkov

We present deterministic polynomial-space algorithms that solve Max 2-SAT on $n$ variables exactly in time $\Ostar(2^{(1-γ)n})$, for a fixed $γ>0$, on several classes of instances whose clause density may grow with $n$. Our main tool extends the classic DPLL branching algorithm. When the search gives a variable its less promising value, comparing the two values of the variable yields a pruning constraint that is satisfied by some optimal assignment. Accumulating these constraints along each branch prunes all but an exponentially small fraction of the assignments. The classes are formulas with many biased variables, semirandom 2-CNF formulas, and Max-Cut on regular expander graphs and on graphs generated by a stochastic block model. In a semirandom formula, the pairs of variables that may share a clause are arbitrary, and the clauses on these pairs are random. For semirandom formulas and block-model graphs, the algorithms are still exact on every input, and the time bound holds with high probability over the input. To our knowledge, these are the first polynomial-space algorithms with such a running time for nontrivial classes of dense Max 2-SAT instances. Beyond these classes, the pruning constraints can be added to any branching algorithm for Max 2-SAT, and we expect them to be of practical relevance for general formulas, in particular for sparse ones, where each constraint involves only a few variables.

item.title: Dimension Reduction and Coresets for Min-Sum $k$-Clustering
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: streaming algorithm

Authors: Asaf Dallal, Robert Krauthgamer

The min-sum $k$-clustering problem asks to partition an input of $n$ points into $k$ clusters so as to minimize the total pairwise distance within clusters. It is a natural alternative to center-based objectives when the data is not well captured by a small set of representative points. We study for this problem two standard sketching methods, dimension reduction and coresets, which represent the input more compactly while preserving the min-sum cost of every $k$-partition up to $1\pm\varepsilon$ factor. Our first contribution addresses dimension reduction in Euclidean space. The Johnson-Lindenstrauss (JL) Lemma readily implies that a random linear map to target dimension $t=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$ preserves, with high probability, the min-sum cost of all $k$-partitions. We show that target dimension $t=O(\varepsilon^{-2}(ddim\cdot\log(1/\varepsilon)+\log k+\log\log n))$ suffices for Euclidean inputs of doubling dimension at most $ddim$, and moreover this bound is nearly optimal. We also show that target dimension $t=O(\varepsilon^{-2}(\log(1/\varepsilon)+\log k+\logΔ))$ suffices for Euclidean inputs of aspect ratio at most $Δ$. Our second contribution is to design the first $\varepsilon$-coreset for metric min-sum $k$-clustering. It is actually a movement-based coreset, has size $(1/\varepsilon)^{O(ddim)} k\log n$ for inputs of doubling dimension at most $ddim$, and can be constructed in randomized near-linear-time. We further use these coresets to design streaming algorithms for the problem.

item.title: Upper Bounds for CSP Non-redundancy via Locally Decodable Codes
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Joshua Brakensiek, David Conlon, Venkatesan Guruswami, Xiaoyu He, Jiaxi Nie, Maya Sankar, Hung-Hsun Hans Yu

In the study of constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs), the non-redundancy of a relation measures the maximum number of clauses in a CSP instance which can be logically independent. In the last few years, CSP non-redundancy has found a number of applications including in query complexity, sparsification, kernelization and streaming. In this paper, we present a novel technique for upper-bounding the non-redundancy of some relations using locally decodable codes (LDCs) and locally correctable codes (LCCs). More precisely, known limitations on the structure of 2-query LDCs and LCCs can be translated into limitations on the size of certain non-redundant CSP instances. This technique builds on a technique used by Brakensiek and Guruswami [STOC 2025] to bound non-redundancy via techniques from matching vector codes. Using LDCs and LCCs, we give improved upper bounds on non-redundancy of the BCK predicate pioneered by Bessiere, Carbonnel, and Katsirelos [AAAI 2020] as well as its well-studied Boolean variant. We also give the first example of a Boolean predicate whose non-redundancy is provably not of the form $n^{k\pm o(1)}$ for some positive integer $k$.

item.title: Directed Cut-Query Complexity of Finding a King
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Ziad Ismaili Alaoui, Oded Lachish, Nikhil S. Mande

A king in a tournament is a vertex from which every other vertex is reachable by a directed path of length at most two. We study the deterministic query complexity of finding a king when a query specifies a set of vertices and returns the number of edges directed from that set to its complement. We prove that this complexity is $Θ(n)$ for $n$-vertex tournaments. To show this, we first show that every correct deterministic algorithm in this model must output a maximum-outdegree vertex, even though a king need not have maximum outdegree. We then give an adversary whose answers, after too few queries, remain consistent with a tournament in which the algorithm's output does not have maximum outdegree.

item.title: Galactus the Devourer
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sublinear

Hi there, argmin readers! Today’s post is about the history of failing to rigorously define efficiency in computer science. Like my previous post on Fourier transforms, it’s more technical than usual, but I tried to make it as accessible as possible.

I’ve always been fascinated by this pernicious pattern in the practice of applied mathematics, which I wrote about here a few weeks ago:

Applied mathematicians often need to build a giant scaffolding of mathematical modeling to solve a problem. This scaffolding creates new mathematical puzzles that aren’t directly connected to the original problem of interest, but that entice problem solvers. You’ll then see dozens of follow-up papers solving the puzzles but forgetting the problem we cared about in the first place.

There is probably no better example of such forgetting than the field of complexity theory.

In 1965, Jack Edmonds came up with a clever way to find a maximum matching in a graph. He wanted to argue that his algorithm could be computed “efficiently,” as the procedure was a bit complicated and required a computer to run. But he found he didn’t have the language to describe what it would mean for an algorithm to be efficient. In Section 2 of his paper, named “Digression,” he wrote,

According to the dictionary, “efficient” means “adequate in operation or performance.” This is roughly the meaning I want—in the sense that it is conceivable for maximum matching to have no efficient algorithm. Perhaps a better word is “good.”

I am claiming, as a mathematical result, the existence of a good algorithm.

Edmonds noted that he could enumerate every possible solution to the matching problem and find the largest one. This would be a correct algorithm. However, the number of total matchings is exponentially large in the size of the graph. Blindly writing all possible matchings down and picking the one that achieved the maximum was a “not good” algorithm. You might call it a “bad” algorithm. His new procedure was vastly more efficient.

So Edmonds spent two pages constructing a definition of good. He demanded that everyone agree on a reasonable definition for a problem size. For his matching problem, he said the size was the number of vertices plus the number of edges in the graph. A good algorithm would then have a running time upper-bounded by some well-defined function of that size, no matter how large the instance. He demanded that the running-time bound hold for every conceivable size, because he feared someone might rig the problem by planting a few small instances that were unnaturally hard.

Edmonds wasn’t completely satisfied with this definition. Indeed, he wrote:

It would be unfortunate for any rigid criterion to inhibit the practical development of algorithms which are either not known or known not to conform nicely to the criterion. Many of the best algorithmic ideas known today would suffer by such theoretical pedantry. In fact, an outstanding open question is, essentially: “how good” is a particular algorithm for linear programming, the simplex method? And, on the other hand, many important algorithmic ideas in electrical switching theory are obviously not “good” in our sense.1

With this caveat noted, he concluded his digression by announcing the complexity of his new blossom algorithm: “An upper bound on the order of difficulty of the matching algorithm is n4, where n is the number of vertices in the graph.”

Edmonds did not make any further arguments for what he meant by good. He asserted that exponential time is bad. For most algorithm designers, linear time, proportional to the input length, was naturally excellent. Moreover, our grade-school multiplication algorithm took quadratic time (multiply two three-digit numbers out by hand like you were taught in school and count the number of digits you write down when you calculate it), and that seemed pretty good. Edmonds had a matching algorithm that required a quartic number of operations. To later formalists like Richard Karp, it seemed like a “polynomial” number of operations was a reasonable definition for goodness. Polynomial time is good. Exponential time is bad. This created the field of complexity theory, with the goal of proving that all sorts of algorithms run in polynomial time and characterizing the problems for which no polynomial-time algorithm existed.

But polynomial time probably haunted Edmonds. It is not a “good” algorithm if your procedure scales like n1000, even if this is technically a polynomial. More absurdly,

is a polynomial bigger than the exponential function 2n for any n we could ever encounter. Polynomial was always an imperfect definition of good, but we ran with it. Thousands of papers later, we just have a zoo of confusing complexity results unmoored from the realities of computation.

Indeed, asymptotic thinking about how polynomials differ from exponentials enables the bad habit of designing “galactic algorithms,” conceptual procedures with running times so large they could never be implemented in our universe. I mentioned these in my earlier post about OpenAI’s Faster Fourier Transform.

This brings me back to our beneficent friends at OpenAI. This week they declared their latest breakthrough in theoretical computer science. They provided an algorithm for the satisfiability problem that ran in “subexponential time.” Satisfiability is one of the most well-known “NP complete problems, and I don’t want to go into the details of P vs NP today, but suffice it to say that you would win a Clay Millennium Prize if you could find a polynomial-time algorithm for satisfiability.2

Now, subexponential time does not mean polynomial time. It merely means that the running time can be bounded as

Where n is the problem size, and f is a “sublinear” function, meaning the limit of f(n)/n goes to zero as n goes to infinity.

Indeed, in the case of OpenAI’s new algorithm for the satisfiability problem, the bound was

For some unspecified constant numbers d and C. Ugly as this expression is, this was touted on Twitter as the biggest moment in theoretical computer science in 50 years. It was covered all over the tech press this week. OpenAI clearly wanted us to think it was a big fucking deal. And many theoretical computer scientists took to social media to agree.

Since it was such a big deal, I wanted to see if I could understand the algorithm a bit. Of course, as I’ve told all of you, we’re not supposed to read these papers. We’re supposed to ask ChatGPT what they say. And ChatGPT told me there was a catch.

The derived algorithm runs exhaustive search—the algorithm Edmonds declared bad in 1965—if the number of variables is less than 10^10,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000.

This is a completely unfathomable number.3 There are something like 10^80 atoms in the universe. That’s 10^9,999,999,999,999,999,999,999,920 times smaller. Up until this barely finite threshold, the magic new algorithm calls an exponential-time subroutine. For any problem that we could ever consider, the procedure is exponential time. The “result” is that only in some bizarre, unknowable neighborhood of infinity, satisfiability problems are solved in subexponential time.

The claimed subexponential algorithm for satisfiability is definitive evidence that our definition of efficient was even worse than we thought it was 50 years ago. The answer tells us nothing about efficiency or goodness. Sometimes you need to answer your question to realize you wanted something else.

I’m not a betting man, but I have a prediction. It’s going to turn out that P=NP in some galactic sense, and all we’ll learn is that we spent fifty years answering the wrong question.

Subscribe now

1

It’s funny that Edmonds references the simplex algorithm in his musings here. The simplex algorithm is the most important algorithm ever invented, and we now know that, technically speaking, its running time is exponential. Most of the time it’s fast, but you can construct weird cases where it takes an exponential number of steps. And yet, it is deployed all over the globe, determining optimal programs for exponentially diverse applications in optimization. Edmonds foresaw this sharp disconnect between theory and practice in 1965!

2

What’s particularly ironic is that we have incredibly efficient algorithms to solve industrial-scale satisfiability problems. Conventional computers can solve problems with millions of variables and millions of clauses. This guy at Intel solved a problem with a billion variables and 4 billion clauses in a day.

3

I confirmed this crazy number by plugging the paper into Claude. ChatGPT and Claude hate each other, so if they agree, it must be true.

By Ben Recht

item.title: Stochastic Minimum Spanning Tree Identification with Binary Weights
item.description:
Filter match: person: sanjeev khanna

Authors: Haya Diwan, Lisa Hellerstein, Sanjeev Khanna, Junkai Song

We introduce the Stochastic MST Identification Problem, with binary weights. In this problem, we need to identify a minimum spanning tree (MST) of a graph, each of whose edge weights is either 0 or 1. The weight of each edge $e$ is a random variable which is 1 with probability $p_e$ and 0 with probability $1-p_e$. The probability $p_e$ is given for each edge $e$, but the realized weight of an edge can only be determined by querying the edge. The problem is then to determine a strategy for querying the edges of the graph that minimizes the expected number of queries that need to be performed until we can identify a subset of edges that form an MST of the graph. We address both adaptive and non-adaptive versions of this problem. For the non-adaptive version of our Stochastic MST Identification problem, we give an $O(\log E)$-approximation algorithm via a reduction to submodular ranking. For the adaptive version, we show that solving the problem is trivial when all $p_e$ are equal to 1/2, because of a relation to the Tutte polynomial. However, computing the expected cost of an optimal querying strategy is #P-hard, even when all $p_e$ equal $\frac{1}{2}$. For arbitrary $p_e$ values, we present a constant-factor approximation algorithm for simple planar graphs. We investigate the question of whether the submodular goal value approach of Deshpande et al. could be used to achieve a $\log$-factor approximation algorithm that would work for arbitrary $p_e$ values and general graphs. In this context, we address the structural question of determining optimal submodular goal values for MST identification in graphs.

item.title: A Better Lower Bound for Sublinear Metric Steiner Tree
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sublinear

Authors: Sepideh Mahabadi, Jakub Tarnawski, Ali Vakilian

In the metric Steiner tree problem, we are given an $n$-point metric space $(V,w)$ and a set of terminals $T\subseteq V$, and we are interested in the smallest total weight $\mathsf{st}(V,T,w)$ of a tree that contains every terminal and may also use points of $V\setminus T$. We work in the distance-oracle model: the algorithm knows $V$ and $T$ in advance and learns $w$ only by querying a single entry $w(u,v)$ at a time. The goal is to estimate $\mathsf{st}(V,T,w)$ with the minimum number of queries. A factor of $2$ is achievable with nearly linear number of queries, so the interesting question is the query complexity of algorithms with an approximation ratio strictly below $2$. We prove that for every fixed $η\in(0,1)$, every randomized $(2-η)$-approximation algorithm must make more than $\widetildeΩ(n^{7/5})$ queries, improving upon the previously known bound of $\widetildeΩ(n^{6/5})$. Given that the best known upper bound shows that $\widetilde O(n^{5/3})$ queries suffice, the exponent of this problem now lies between $7/5$ and $5/3$, up to logarithmic factors.

item.title: A Fully Polynomial Randomized Approximation Scheme for Hypergraph Unreliability
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: minimum cut

Authors: Zhijie Zheng

We give a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for all-terminal unreliability in explicitly represented undirected hypergraphs of arbitrary rank. The algorithm estimates the probability that independent hyperedge failures disconnect the hypergraph, allowing a different rational failure probability for every edge. For a common failure probability, this improves the quasi-polynomial approximation schemes of Cen, Li, and Panigrahi to polynomial time and answers the polynomial-time approximation question reiterated in their subsequent work on graphs. The construction turns their representative-survival bound into an importance sampler whose relative second moment is bounded solely in terms of the number of vertices. We protect one randomly chosen representative pair during contraction, correct the path likelihood, and divide by the number of pairs surviving at the end. The resulting unbiased estimator has relative second moment at most $\binom n2$, even when unreliability is exponentially small. A minimum-cut normalization makes this estimator implementable with polynomially bounded precision: the residual likelihood becomes a survival probability in an auxiliary absorbing process, which admits rational discretization with a fixed random-bit budget. Logarithmic rate rounding and an exact weighted minimum cut extend the construction to unequal rational failure probabilities. The algorithm's worst-case running time and random-bit usage are polynomial in the input length, the inverse relative error, and $\log(1/δ)$ for confidence $1-δ$.

item.title: Degree Realization with Maximum Matching
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: maximum matching

Authors: Amotz Bar-Noy, Igor Kalinichev, David Peleg, Dror Rawitz

The Maximum Matching Degree Realization problem requires, for a sequence $d$ of $n$ positive integers, to compute a realizing graph(whose degree sequence corresponds to $d$) with the maximum possible matching. We present a polynomial-time algorithm for this problem. The decision version of this problem requires to determine whether a sequence $d$ admits a realization with a matching of size $ν$ (without computing such a realization). Recently, it was shown that it can be done by verifying a series of inequalities. We improve the existing characterization by reducing the number of inequalities.

item.title: Revisiting the directed pathwidth of h-semicomplete digraphs
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sublinear

Authors: Guilherme C. M. Gomes, Raul Lopes, Matthias Mnich

A digraph is $h$-semicomplete if every vertex has at most $h$ non-neighbors. In semicomplete digraphs, $k$-triples are obstructions to bounded directed pathwidth with many algorithmic applications: Fradkin and Seymour [JCTB 2013] showed that a large triple contains a subdivision of every small digraph, and triples were used for irrelevant vertex arguments in routing problems by Fomin and Pilipczuk [JCTB 2019] and Gomes, Lopes, and Sau [ICALP 2025]. Fradkin and Seymour also showed that there is a function $f(k)$ such that every semicomplete digraph of directed pathwidth at least $f(k)$ contains a $k$-triple, and their proof gives $f(k)$ triply exponential in $k$. For $h$-semicomplete digraphs, a result of Kitsunai et al. [ESA 2015] also yields a $k$-triple, but only existentially, and finding one in fixed-parameter time remained open. We improve the bound on $f(k)$ to a single exponential and extend the result to $h$-semicomplete digraphs: we show that every $h$-semicomplete digraph of directed pathwidth greater than $(h+1) \cdot k \cdot 2^{27k+9}$ contains a $k$-triple, which we find in polynomial time, and no bound subexponential in $k$ or sublinear in $h$ is possible. We also extend the approximation algorithm for directed pathwidth of Fomin and Pilipczuk to $h$-semicomplete digraphs, so its certificates of large directed pathwidth remain valid. Our proof is much shorter than the analysis of Kitsunai et al., and while their algorithm is exact, ours runs in polynomial time. As an application, we show that Arc-Disjoint Paths on $h$-semicomplete digraphs is fixed-parameter tractable parameterized by the number of paths and $h$, generalizing the semicomplete case. Finally, unlike in semicomplete digraphs, directed pathwidth does not bound directed cliquewidth: for every $k$, some acyclic $1$-semicomplete digraph, so of directed pathwidth zero, has directed cliquewidth at least $k$.

item.title: Optimal Online Weighted Connectivity Augmentation
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: connectivity

Authors: Mohit Garg, Felix Hommelsheim, Alexander Lindermayr

In the online Weighted Connectivity Augmentation Problem (WCAP), we are given a $k$-edge-connected graph on $n$ vertices and a set of additional edges, called links, with nonnegative costs. Pairs of vertices arrive one by one, and an online algorithm must immediately and irrevocably buy links so that each pair becomes $(k+1)$-edge-connected. The goal is to minimize the total cost of the purchased links. We obtain a deterministic polynomial-time $O(\log n)$-competitive algorithm for WCAP, improving the previous $O(\log^2 n)$ bound (SODA 2026). Our bound is asymptotically optimal, even for randomized algorithms in the random-order model. The general problem reduces to the case where the underlying graph is a cycle, for which link costs in $\{0,1\}$ already yield an $Ω(\log n)$ lower bound. Surprisingly, for unit costs on a cycle, we obtain a deterministic polynomial-time $4$-competitive algorithm, improving the previous $O(\log n)$ bound (SODA 2026), and prove that this ratio is optimal among deterministic algorithms. Thus, with unit costs, cycles are easier than trees, where the optimal competitive ratio is $Θ(\log n)$.

item.title: Catalytic space-efficient algorithms for Distance and Determinant
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sublinear

Authors: Srijan Chakraborty, Samir Datta, Kushagra Shandilya

Catalytic computation reuses potentially large but in-use space (or catalytic space) which must be restored to its initial contents while the clean space is small. This allows all problems in $\mathsf{NL}$ and even larger classes to be in catalytic logspace [Buhrman et al, STOC2014]. In [Chmel et al, CCC2026] the catalytic space for reachability was restricted to sublinear space (specifically, $n \big/ 2^{θ(\sqrt{\log n})}$ space) while remaining in polynomial time. This matches the non-catalytic bounds from [Barnes et al, SICOMP1998]. We extend the reachability bound to shortest distance, proving a simultaneous sublinear catalytic space and polynomial time bound (henceforth called, sublinear $\mathsf{CLP}$). This is the first simultaneous sublinear space and polynomial time bound for distance even without the catalytic discipline. Moreover, our bound works even for polynomially weighted graphs. Along the way we prove simultaneous near linear catalytic space ($\mathcal{O}(n\log^{O(1)}{n})$) and polynomial time bounds for the determinant. We also show some applications to planar matching problems. Our starting point was catalytic computation of reachability in directed graphs by [Cook-Pyne, ITCS2026]. [Edenhofer, arXiv:2602.21088] used it to give a tradeoff between catalytic and non-catalytic space, while [Chmel et al, CCC2026] compress the graph to a smaller graph preserving $s,t$-reachability to achieve a smaller space bound. All three can be modified to yield an algorithm for unweighted distance. Our contribution is to define an approximation to the walk polynomial in weighted graphs that allows us to infer weighted $s,t$-distance in sublinear $\mathsf{CLP}$. We do so by non-trivially combining elements from each of the above three papers.

item.title: $k$-Center under Weak and Strong Distance Oracles with an Application to Minimum Sum of Radii Clustering
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Zachary Friggstad, Mahya Jamshidian, Ali Vakilian

In the weak-strong distance oracle model of Bateni, Dharangutte, Jayaram and Wang (COLT 2024), a metric $(X,d)$ on $n$ points is accessed through two oracles: a cheap weak oracle that returns each queried distance correctly with probability $1-δ$ and permits arbitrary values on corrupted pairs, chosen by an adversary who knows the entire metric and all corrupted pairs, and an expensive strong oracle that reveals a point exactly. The goal is to cluster well while making as few strong queries as possible. Our main result is a $(6+\varepsilon)$-approximation for $k$-center using $O(k\log n\log(\varepsilon^{-1}\log n))$ strong point queries, for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$. This improves both the $(14+\varepsilon)$ approximation factor and the $O(k\log^2 n\log(\varepsilon^{-1}\log n))$ query bound of Bateni et al. It also improves the query complexity of the recent $(6+\varepsilon)$-approximation of Pradhan, Bhattacharya and Jaiswal (AISTATS 2026), in the variant of the model they study. Our algorithm outputs an explicitly known sketch of an otherwise unknown metric: a concrete metric on at most $k$ points that a downstream algorithm can compute with directly, with no further queries and no noise. As an application, we give a simple FPT algorithm for Minimum Sum of Radii (MSR) that returns a constant-factor solution using $2^{O(k\log k)}\cdot O(\log n\log\log n)$ strong queries. We complement the upper bound with an $Ω(k\log(n/k))$ lower bound for $k$-center with assignment that holds for row-local algorithms. These algorithms assign two unqueried points to the same center whenever their weak distances to the strong-queried points are exactly the same. Our algorithm and those of Bateni et al. and Pradhan et al. are all row-local, so our query bound is optimal for this class up to the $O(\log\log n)$ factor.

item.title: Testing MAX-CUT in the Adjacency Matrix Model: Tight Non-Adaptive Bounds and a Cubic Adaptive Lower Bound
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Songhua He

We study the query complexity of approximating the MAX-CUT value to additive error $\varepsilon n^2$ in the adjacency matrix model. This was one of the first problems studied in the area of graph property testing [GGR, JACM'1998]. Previously, the best known upper bound for both adaptive and non-adaptive algorithms was $O(1/\varepsilon^6)$ [MS, SODA'2008; GMRS, ICALP'2022]. The only known lower bound was a trivial $Ω(1/\varepsilon^2)$ bound. We close this gap from both sides for non-adaptive algorithms, proving that its query complexity is exactly $Θ(1/\varepsilon^4)$. We also prove an adaptive $Ω(1/\varepsilon^3)$ lower bound. Our upper bound is achieved by a canonical tester that samples $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ vertices in expectation and outputs the rescaled MAX-CUT value of the induced subgraph. We prove its correctness by applying spectral truncation to the adjacency matrix, using a geometric argument to control the sampling error of the retained low-rank part and a cut-norm restriction estimate [RV, JACM'2007] for the remainder. As an application, an analogous proof also yields a tight $O(1/\varepsilon^4)$ non-adaptive query upper bound for MAX-2CSP. For our lower bounds, we show indistinguishability between a uniform random graph and a distribution that plants a hidden partition. For the non-adaptive lower bound, we observe that one plus the $χ^2$-divergence between the query transcript distributions is exactly a normalized Ising partition function, which can be bounded using Boolean hypercontractivity. For the adaptive lower bound, we view each query through the algorithm's ability to predict whether its endpoints lie in the same part of the hidden partition. We bound the combined advantage of these predictions using the completed transcript, which lets us analyze the adaptively chosen pairs together despite their dependence on earlier answers.

item.title: Shared Randomness and Parallel Rounds in Permutation Sampling
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: local computation

Authors: Haoxiang Huang

We study the shared randomness needed to sample a uniform permutation in parallel output rounds. Coordinates committed in the same round are independent conditional on the complete history and the current shared choice. Previous outputs are public; local computation and private randomness are free. We charge each shared choice by the logarithm of its conditional support size and sum these costs along the worst execution path. At every fixed round density $ρ\in(0,1)$, the optimal limiting total-variation error under any $o(n)$ shared budget matches the conditional-marginal optimum, even with arbitrary local kernels and adaptive coordination. A fixed improvement requires linear cost. For exact sampling in $R=Θ(n)$ rounds, the optimum is $nΦ(R/n)+O(\log n)$, where $Φ$ linearly interpolates $Φ(1/q)=\log q$. A protocol attaining this rate uses an initial seed and at most one further binary shared choice. When $\lceil n/2\rceil\le R\le n$, the finite optimum is $\log\binom{2(n-R)}{n-R}$, attained by an initial seed alone. The approximate converse uses an entropy inequality for sparse injections to control overlap with the target. The exact construction reuses randomness retained in a shared label partition after the first-stage outputs are exposed.

item.title: Fluid Limits and Upper Bounds for Randomized Greedy Matching
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: maximum matching

Authors: Sayan Mukherjee

The Modified Randomized Greedy (MRG) algorithm [Tinhofer (1984), Aronson-Dyer-Frieze-Suen (1995)] is a classical greedy algorithm for finding approximate maximum matchings. MRG repeatedly picks a uniformly random unmatched vertex and matches it to a uniformly random unmatched neighbor, if one exists. Since 1991, the best upper bound on its approximation ratio has been $2/3$, given by the Bomb graphs of [Dyer and Frieze (1991)]. We improve this bound to $0.6569$ on general graphs and $0.6607$ on bipartite graphs. Our constructions consist of copies of small gadgets, with specified vertex classes joined completely. We track each algorithm by counting gadget copies with each possible configuration of remaining vertices. Wormald's differential equation method [Wormald (1995)] shows that these counts, scaled by the size parameter of the construction, converge to a deterministic trajectory known as the \textit{fluid limit}, which is described by ordinary differential equations. This fluid limit approximation holds while the relevant vertex classes have positive density, and so we devise a separate counting argument determines the contribution from the end of the run. Furthermore, we apply our framework to Random Decision Order (RDO), in which vertices are processed in uniformly random order and choose unmatched neighbors according to fixed adversarial preferences. On bipartite graphs, we determine the exact limiting ratio on the Double-Bomb family of [Tang-Wu-Zhang (2020)]. Its minimum is $31/48$, confirming their numerical estimate of about $0.646$.On general graphs, we improve their upper bound of $5/8$, given by the paw graph, to $0.5946$ on a new family. Finally, we give one possible explanation for why $2/3$ seemed to be optimal for MRG in the concluding remarks.

item.title: Monotone Local Search with Sample-Dependent Running Times
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: connectivity

Authors: Serge Gaspers

Monotone Local Search turns an algorithm that extends a given partial solution into an algorithm that finds a solution from scratch: sample a few elements, hope that they lie in an unknown solution, and complete them. Its known analyses bound every call of the extension algorithm by a worst-case time that depends only on the number of sampled elements, and Esmer et al. (SODA 2024) showed that no algorithm that uses the extension algorithm as a black box with this running time beats the original form by more than a polynomial factor. We let this running time depend on the actual sample. If the extension algorithm decides in time $O^*(2^{g(I,X,k)})$, for a polynomial-time computable $g$, whether a sample $X$ can be completed to a solution with at most $k$ elements, our main theorem gives a randomized algorithm with one-sided error in time $O^*(2^{ψn})$ whenever, for some solution $S$ of size $k$ and some $t$, the exponential moment $\sum_{X\subseteq S,|X|=t}2^{-g(I,X,k)}$ is at least $2^{-ψn}\binom{n}{t}$. A corollary, multivariate Monotone Local Search, generalizes the theorems of Fomin et al. (STOC 2016, J. ACM 2019) and of Gaspers and Lee (ICALP 2017). For Max Leaf Spanning Tree and, equivalently, Connected Dominating Set, the previous best polynomial-space bound is $O^*(1.8619^n)$. Completing a sample is a Steiner tree problem, solved in time exponential in the number of terminals, which varies strongly with the sample. We obtain a randomized polynomial-space algorithm in time $O(1.6991^n)$ and a deterministic one in time $(\sqrt5-\frac12)^n 2^{o(n)}=O(1.7361^n)$. For connectivity problems in which the extension algorithm's running time doubles with every component of the sample, an analysis through a partition function gives randomized polynomial-space algorithms in time $O^*(1.8^n)$ for Connected Feedback Vertex Set and $O(1.6444^n)$ for Connected Vertex Cover.

item.title: Faster Semi-Streaming and Dynamic Approximate Maximum Weight Matchings in General Graphs: A Unified Framework
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: semi-streaming

Authors: Jiale Chen

We study the $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximate maximum weight matching problem in general graphs with $n$ vertices and integer edge weights in $[1,W]$. For $W=n^{O(1)}$, we obtain faster algorithms in the semi-streaming and dynamic settings: (1) Semi-streaming: Deterministic $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$-pass and $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\varepsilon))$-pass algorithms for unweighted and weighted matching. (2) Incremental: A deterministic algorithm for weighted matching processing $m$ edge insertions in total time $O((m\varepsilon^{-3}+n\varepsilon^{-6})\log^3 n)$. (3) Decremental: A randomized algorithm for weighted matching processing all edge deletions from an $m$-edge graph in total time $O((m\varepsilon^{-8}+n\varepsilon^{-47})\log^{O(1)}n)$ with high probability. (4) Fully dynamic: A deterministic reduction from weighted matching in general graphs to unweighted matching in bipartite graphs incurring $O(\varepsilon^{-4}\log^{O(1)}(1/\varepsilon))$ multiplicative update-time overhead, independent of $n$. Underlying these results is a unified framework that reduces the problem to repeatedly solving two simpler matching subproblems: a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximate maximum weight matching on a sparse subgraph with $O(n/\varepsilon)$ edges, and a constant approximation on the remaining edges. The framework builds on dual entropy regularization, a smoothing technique underlying efficient solvers for packing linear programs. To handle the exponentially many odd-set constraints, we adapt the smoothing technique to regularize only the vertex duals and develop a new cut partition that preserves odd-set feasibility during optimization.

item.title: Finding and Certifying Weighted Minimum Cuts with Cut Queries
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Troy Lee

We study the deterministic and nondeterministic cut query complexity of minimum cut in undirected graphs with arbitrary nonnegative edge weights. For the nondeterministic case, we show that every $n$-vertex graph has an $O(n\log^2(2n))$-query certificate of its exact global minimum-cut value, such that any other nonnegatively weighted graph on the same vertex set that agrees on these queries has the same minimum cut value. A key ingredient is a way to certify a maximum $s$--$t$ flow value with only $O(n)$ cut queries. For the deterministic case we give an algorithm that finds an exact global minimum cut using $O(n^{3/2}\log^3(2n)(\log\log(2n))^2)$ cut queries. Previously no $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ deterministic bound was known for arbitrary nonnegatively weighted graphs. The algorithm follows Karger's two-respecting tree approach. The key new ingredient is a deterministic construction of a weak skeleton of the input graph $G$: an explicit weighted graph $H$ in which every minimum cut of $G$ is a $5/4$-approximate minimum cut.

item.title: Optimal Sample Complexity for Max-Cut
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: max-cut

Authors: Itamar Bender, Robert Krauthgamer

We determine the optimal sample size for constructing value coresets for Max-Cut via uniform vertex sampling. That is, sampling $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ vertices uniformly at random in $n$-vertex graphs with edge weights in $[0,1]$ yields a reweighted subgraph whose Max-Cut value is an additive $\varepsilon n^2$-approximation to that of the original graph, with constant success probability. This improves the previously known $O(\varepsilon^{-4})$ upper bound and matches the known lower bound. The same guarantee holds also for importance sampling, where vertices are sampled proportionally to their weighted degrees, and we further prove a matching lower bound for this sampling method. Our analysis extends directly to metric Max-Cut, showing that importance sampling of $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ vertices yields $(1\pm\varepsilon)$-approximation to the Max-Cut value, and to Max-Cut in graphs with edge weights in $[0,1]$ and average weighted degree $\bar d$, achieving the same $(1\pm\varepsilon)$-approximation by either uniform or importance sampling of $O(\varepsilon^{-2}n/\bar d)$ vertices. We additionally show how to use this coreset to recover a cut of expected value at least $OPT-\varepsilon n^2$, by making $O(n\varepsilon^{-2})$ additional edge-weight queries. Finally, our result extends to Max-$r$-Cut, giving an additive $\varepsilon n^2$-approximation using a sample of $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(2r))$ vertices.

item.title: Stochastic Matching with Polynomial Degree
item.description:
Filter match: person: soheil behnezhad

Authors: Soheil Behnezhad

We study the stochastic matching problem, where a graph $G$ is known in advance, but each edge survives independently with probability $p$. The goal is to select a subgraph $H$ of small maximum degree before seeing the surviving edges, while preserving a $(1-ε)$ fraction of the expected maximum matching size. This problem has received significant attention due to its numerous applications in kidney exchange, labor markets, and online dating. In this paper, we show there is always a subgraph $H \subseteq G$ achieving a $(1-ε)$-approximation while having a maximum degree of at most $O\left(\frac{\log(1/ε)}{ε^4} \cdot \frac{1}{p}\right).$ This resolves a major conjecture of the literature, first stated by [BDH, STOC'20], that $poly(\frac{1}{εp})$ degrees suffice. The best previous bound was $(1/p)^{\exp((1/ε)\log(1/ε))}$ by [ABGR, STOC'25]. The key to this result is a lemma of independent interest that any distribution over the matchings of a stochastic graph can be transformed to another distribution which matches each vertex with exactly the same probability, but exhibits extremely low total pairwise correlation.

item.title: Square-Root Pass Semi-Streaming Algorithms for Digraph Problems
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: streaming algorithm

Authors: Prantar Ghosh, Amirhossein Janfaza

We study directed graph problems in the semi-streaming model where we are restricted to $\widetilde{O}(n):=O(n\cdot \text{polylog}(n))$ space for processing the edge stream of an $n$-node graph and can make one or a few passes to solve the given problem. A longstanding open problem in multipass streaming is determining the number of semi-streaming passes needed to solve directed $s,t$-reachability: there is an exponential gap---$Ω(\log n/\log \log n)$ vs $n^{1/2+o(1)}$---between the best-known lower and upper bounds. Several related fundamental digraph problems, e.g., topological sorting, acyclicity testing, and decomposition into strongly connected components (SCCs), are known to have the same semi-streaming pass lower bound. However, no $o(n/\text{polylog}(n))$-pass upper bound was known for any of them. Our main result achieves an $n^{1/2+o(1)}$-pass semi-streaming algorithm for each of these problems. As a corollary, we get algorithms with the same pass and space usage for a broad class of DAG problems that admit a certain form of dynamic program over a topological ordering. This class includes weighted single-source shortest paths, longest paths, max-outdegree+1 coloring, and constructing a lexicographically-first DFS (depth-first search) forest. Our algorithm for the last problem can be seen as a generalization of our results on topological sorting and acyclicity testing: recall that standard textbook algorithms for these problems use DFS as a subroutine. Our algorithms are optimal up to an $n^{o(1)}$ factor in passes under the reasonable conjecture that $s,t$-reachability requires $Ω(\sqrt{n})$ semi-streaming passes. However, using the fact that our algorithms can be parameterized by the number of passes taken by topological sorting or single-source reachability algorithms, we prove stronger lower bounds for some of the problems even under weaker conjectures.

item.title: Near-Optimal Space and Time Cut Sparsification in Turnstile Streams
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: turnstile stream

Authors: Honghao Lin, Vahab Mirrokni, David P. Woodruff

A seminal result of Ahn, Guha, and McGregor (PODS'12) showed that a cut sparsifier of an unweighted graph can be computed from a near-linear number of linear measurements. Later work extended this to spectral sparsifiers (Kapralov et al., FOCS'14) and to near-linear recovery time (Kapralov et al., SODA'20). For weighted graphs, these sketches rely on grouping edges by weight, which general turnstile streams do not allow. Chen, Khanna, and Li (FOCS'22) removed this limitation, using $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^3)$ bits of space. We improve the space to $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^2)$ bits. Our algorithm makes one pass over a general turnstile stream of a weighted graph, processes each update in $\tilde{O}(1)$ time, and recovers, in $\tilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^2)$ time, a reweighted subgraph with $O(n\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2 n)$ edges that preserves every cut within a factor of $1\pm\varepsilon$. Its space, update time, and recovery time are all optimal up to polylogarithmic factors.

item.title: A Decomposition Theorem and a Simple Algorithm for Contraction Fixed Points
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query algorithm

Authors: Xi Chen, Yuhao Li, Mihalis Yannakakis

We prove a decomposition theorem for the problem of computing an approximate fixed point of a contraction map $f\colon [0,1]^k \to [0,1]^k$ under the $\ell_{\infty}$-norm. After a preliminary version of the decomposition theorem appeared on arXiv [CLY26], Feodorov and Haslebacher [FH26] gave a striking application of the theorem, showing that it can be used to convert any $\operatorname{poly}(k,\log(1/\varepsilon))$-query algorithm with running time $(k\log(1/\varepsilon))^{O(k)}$ into an algorithm with running time $(k\log(1/\varepsilon))^{O(\sqrt{k})}$. They instantiated this framework with an $O(k^2\log(1/\varepsilon))$-query algorithm with the desired running time, thereby obtaining the first subexponential-time algorithm for contraction fixed points under the $\ell_{\infty}$-norm and, via well-known reductions, the first deterministic subexponential-time algorithm for simple stochastic games and mean-payoff games. In addition to the decomposition theorem, as our second main result in this paper, we show that the $O(k\log(1/\varepsilon))$-query algorithm of [CLY25] can be implemented in time $(k\log(1/\varepsilon))^{O(k)}$; our algorithm may be viewed as conceptually simpler compared to the algorithm of [FH26]. A key observation here is that the function constructed in [CLY25], whose fixed points are used as the next query points, turns out to be nonexpansive under the $\ell_{\infty}$-norm, so the brute-force procedure can be replaced by known algorithms for contraction fixed points.

item.title: Subpolynomial-Query Proximal Sampling Beyond Log-Concavity
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

Authors: Wei Guo, Bo Yuan, Ye He, Jiaming Liang, Molei Tao, Yongxin Chen

We study the gradient query complexity of sampling from a density $π(x)\propto\mathrm{e}^{-V(x)}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $V$ has a $β$-Lipschitz gradient but need not be convex. Our approach uses the proximal sampler, which alternates Gaussian perturbation with sampling a position conditional on the noisy observation. We implement its observation chain using the high-order noisy conditional sampler of [OpenAI 2026], obtaining improved dimension dependence under functional inequalities. If $π$ satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality (LSI) with constant $α$, then for every fixed $ν>0$, there is a finite constant $C_ν$ depending only on $ν$ such that the algorithm returns a sample within total-variation distance $\varepsilon$ using at most $C_νκ(d+κ+\varepsilon^{-1}+\|\nabla V(x_0)\|^2/β)^ν$ queries, where $κ=β/α$ and $x_0$ is an arbitrary reference point for initialization. The analysis controls center-dependent local errors along exact proximal histories and removes the final observation noise by conditional decoding. Under a Poincaré inequality (PI), we obtain a corresponding guarantee from a warm start with a known bound on its Rényi divergence. An oracle lower bound shows that a stationary point alone, which suffices under LSI, is insufficient under PI.

item.title: Tilted Convexity and an Exact Offline-Online Separation
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sublinear

Authors: Mohammad Pedramfar, Rajiv Khanna, Christopher John Quinn, Vaneet Aggarwal

Convexity has three equivalent descriptions: support by affine functions, monotonicity of the subdifferential, and increasing secant slopes. We weaken all three by one distortion with parameter $γ\in(0,1]$, which multiplies positive changes by $γ$ and divides negative ones by $γ$. The resulting classes are the convex functions at $γ=1$ and, for $γ<1$, are distinct and nested, with the parameter dropping by at most a square along the chain. For proper lower semicontinuous functions in these classes, the effective domain is convex, local minimizers are global, and the function is locally Lipschitz on the relative interior of its domain. The classes separate offline from online optimization over compact convex sets with efficient projection, with access to function values and bounded support vectors. A smooth member of any class can be minimized to additive accuracy $\varepsilon$ with $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ first-order queries and projections. Online, with nonpositive losses and $α$-regret measured against $α$ times the best fixed point, a polynomial-time algorithm achieves $γ$-regret $O(\sqrt T)$ on the largest class. For every fixed, effectively specified $γ\in(0,1)$ and every $α\in(γ,1]$, no randomized polynomial-time algorithm has sublinear expected $α$-regret unless $\mathbf{NP}=\mathbf{RP}$, already for smooth concave polynomial losses in the smallest class, each minimized by one linear optimization. Thus, unless $\mathbf{NP}=\mathbf{RP}$, $γ$ is the exact online coefficient of each class, while the offline coefficient is one.

item.title: A Circuit Complexity Trichotomy For Regular Languages
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: sublinear

Authors: Stefan Göller, Amaldev Manuel

We establish a trichotomy for the non-uniform, unbounded-fan-in circuit complexity of regular languages: the complexity of every regular language lies in exactly one of $O(1)$, $Ω(\log n)\cap O(\log n\log\log n)$, or $Ω(n)\cap O(n)$. Our main technical contribution is a characterization of the sublinear class in terms of algebra, word congruences, regular expressions, and logic. This class consists precisely of the regular languages computable by constant-depth circuits of size $O(\log^2 n)$, or, equivalently, by circuits of size $O(\log n\log\log n)$ and depth $O((\log\log n)^2)$. Consequently, every regular language of sublinear circuit complexity is definable in $\mathrm{FO}^2[Σ,<,\mathrm{mod}]$, which is contained in wire-linear $\mathbf{AC}^0$. For each of the three classes, deciding membership is $\mathbf{PSPACE}$-complete when the language is specified by a nondeterministic finite automaton. We also obtain a corresponding classification for regular languages with a neutral letter.

item.title:
TR26-292 | Testing Implies Distance Estimation with Polynomial Loss |
Cameron Seth,
Gaia Carenini
item.description:
Filter match: keyword: query complexity

A tester decides whether a graph has a property or is far from having it. A distance estimator asks for more: it must approximately determine how many edges need to be changed. A property is said to be testable if there is a tester with a number of queries bounded independently of the graph's order for each conceivable distance. Similarly, if a property admits an estimator with a number of queries bounded independently of the graph's order, it is said to be estimable. Fischer and Newman proved that, in the dense graph model, every testable property is also estimable. We show that the passage from testing to estimation requires only a polynomial increase in query complexity. This resolves a long-standing open problem in property testing, previously tackled by Fiat and Ron, by Hoppen, Kohayakawa, Lang, Lefmann, and Stagni, and by Gishboliner, Kushnir, and Shapira.
